newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: YUugosv president post vacant for Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: YUugosv president post vacant for Milosevic.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, seeking a fresh power base, is expected to make a smooth transition to Yugoslavia's newly-vacated federal presidency next month, political sources said on Thursday.
Milosevic, the candidate of the ruling Socialist party (SPS), is expected to face little opposition in replacing outgoing President Zoran Lilic, whose term of office expired on Wednesday.
The Serbian constitution forbids Milosevic from seeking a third term as the republic's president.
Candidates for the federal presidency must submit their nominations by July 15 and a president must be elected by the parliament by July 25.
In the interim Srdja Bozovic, speaker of the federal parliament's Upper House, is the acting president.
Milosevic's leftist coalition, which includes the ruling Montenegrin DPS, has 84 seats out of 138 in the Lower House. He also controls 26 seats in the 40-seat Upper House.
Milosevic's nomination by the SPS has been marred only by a rift with reformers within the DPS of Montenegro, Serbia's tiny partner in the federation where it enjoys equal rights.
The DPS agreed on Monday to support his nomination but refused to back proposals for constitutional changes under which Milosevic would be elected by universal suffrage.

It argued the amendments would reduce Montenegro's authority within the federation but in reality the reformers, led by Prime Minister Milo Djukanovic, fear they would give Milosevic the wide powers he is accustomed to in Serbia.
The federal presidency is technically a ceremonial office but diplomats believe Milosevic can expect little obstruction from the Montenegrin mavericks once he takes over.

On the other hand, the Serbian opposition Zajedno coalition, which challenged Milosevic's authority this winter, has collapsed amid bickering over power-sharing and has not yet nominated a candidate for the federal post.
Zajedno mounted massive street demonstrations drawing up to 500,000 people in Belgrade braving bitter colds to protest against fraud at November local elections.
International pressure forced Milosevic to restore Zajedno's victory in Belgrade and 13 other big towns in Serbia.

But the coalition, comprising the Serbian Renewal Movement (SPO), the Democratic Party (DS) and the Civil Alliance has effectively split up as its leaders have traded accusations of selling out to Milosevic.
The dispute is threatening the opposition's chances of capturing the Serbian presidency in elections which may be held as early as September.
